reflection.quote: We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.
reflection.reading:
It's a Thursday in September. Nothing particular is being asked of you today. No milestone, no crisis, no crowd watching to see if you'll hold it together. Just a regular weekday with regular obligations and a regular evening waiting on the other side of it. This is the terrain where sobriety actually gets built.

When I was drinking, I lived for the exceptional days — the Fridays, the trips, the reasons to celebrate or the reasons to cope. Thursdays were something to survive on the way to something else. What I've learned in the years since is that a life is mostly Thursdays. If you can't show up for those, you don't really have a life — you have a series of escapes stitched together by dread. The gift of getting sober isn't that every day becomes remarkable. It's that ordinary days stop feeling like a sentence.

Durant, paraphrasing Aristotle, got it right. You don't become someone you can live with in a single decision. You become that person by making small, boring, unglamorous choices on unremarkable days. Coffee instead of a drink. A walk instead of a scroll. A phone call you didn't want to make. Bed at a reasonable hour. None of it looks like much. All of it is the thing.
reflection.meditation: What is one small, ordinary act today that the person I'm becoming would do?

affirmations: I am building a life out of ordinary days, and that is enough.
Today I have agency over how I respond, even when I don't have control over what happens.
I am becoming someone I can actually live with.

gratitude.prayer: Grateful for a Thursday that doesn't have to be survived. Grateful for a clear head, a body that woke up rested, and the small unremarkable freedoms I used to think I'd have to give up to get here. Grateful for the people who stayed, and the ones I've met since.
gratitude.closing: One more ordinary day. One more quiet win.
